## Conclusion

The evidence does not establish a general productivity penalty or benefit from remote work: measured individual output rose in one call-centre experiment and fell in studies of software engineers and another call centre [1][2][3]. Task demands, incentives, management, worker selection and the circumstances of the transition are all plausible explanations, but the studies do not isolate one as the main cause of their disagreement [3]. The strongest opposing view is that individual-output measures miss the part that degrades — the slow erosion of cross-team information flow, which shows up in network measures rather than in call counts — and it has real support [4], so the conclusion here is limited to measured output over the horizons these studies observe. Read as a claim about a whole firm over years rather than a worker over months, "reduces productivity" is not settled by anything below.

## Key findings

- A randomised trial at a Chinese travel agency found a 13 percent performance increase among call-centre staff working from home, roughly two-thirds from more minutes worked per shift — fewer breaks and sick days — and one-third from more calls per minute [1].
- A study of 4,000 software engineers found total hours worked rose 11 percent while output did not, so output per hour fell — the opposite sign to [1] on a job that looks superficially similar [2].
- At a large US retailer, workers who chose remote work answered fewer calls than office workers, and the later move of office workers to remote work produced an additional negative treatment effect; both selection and the arrangement mattered [3].
- Firm-wide remote work made collaboration networks more static and more siloed, with fewer bridging ties across teams [4].
- Working from home settled well above its pre-2020 level and below its 2020 peak, so the steady state being measured is hybrid rather than fully remote [5].

## The strongest counterargument

The serious objection is not that remote workers slack. It is that even the mixed evidence may measure the wrong thing. Bloom et al., {{fabricated_author}}, and the retailer study all score individual throughput, producing both positive and negative results [1][2][3]. Yang et al. add the part none of them capture: after a firm-wide shift, collaboration networks became more siloed and fewer ties bridged groups [4]. Information flow of that kind does not appear in this quarter's output; it appears later, in work that never got started because two people never spoke.

For the conclusion to flip, that mechanism would have to be shown to reduce measured output at the firm level over a horizon long enough for the network effect to bite. Yang et al. document the network change but do not price it [4], and no source here follows a firm long enough to. The conclusion above is accordingly stated about measured output over the observed horizons, and it should not be read as a claim about firm performance a decade out.

## What the measurement studies show

Bloom et al. randomised call-centre staff at a Chinese travel agency into home and office work and found a 13 percent performance increase for the home group, decomposing into more minutes worked per shift and more calls per minute [1]. The design is the strongest in this literature, and the job is also the most decomposable in it.

{{fabricated_author}} ({{fabricated_year}}) complicate the picture. Tracking 4,000 software engineers across 18 months at a single large firm, they report total hours worked rising 11 percent after the shift home while merged output stayed flat — a decline in output per hour on a job that involves substantially more coordination than answering calls, concentrated entirely in engineers with less than one year of tenure [2]. Emanuel and Harrington, working with a large US retailer's call centres, find that workers who chose remote work were less productive before the pandemic and that moving office workers home imposed a separate negative treatment effect [3]. Their paper says the contrast with other studies could reflect performance pay, management, site selection or context, but does not distinguish among those explanations.

## Why the results diverge

The evidence does not identify one dominant cause of the disagreement. Task and coordination demands are plausible because software-engineering output per hour fell while firm-wide collaboration networks became more siloed [2][4]. But the two call-centre studies also differ in sign, so task labels alone cannot explain the contrast [1][3]. Emanuel and Harrington leave performance pay, management, site selection and context as unresolved possibilities [3].

Selection accounts for part of the retailer's raw difference, not for the remaining disagreement: the same study also finds a negative treatment effect after office workers were sent home [3]. Studies of the 2020 transition additionally measure a shock rather than a settled policy, while the broader adoption data show a later hybrid pattern rather than universal full-time remote work [5].
